items.alt: A Taal street leading to the basilica

children.text: A historic town in Batangas where Taal Basilica, ranked among Asia's largest Catholic churches, stands alongside wooden mansions from the Spanish and American eras that still line the alleys. A day-trip destination for walking between the basilica and heritage-house museums while tasting Taal longganisa and tapa.
Taal is a small town in southwestern Batangas province, at the mouth where the Pansipit River flows from Taal Lake into Balayan Bay. The original settlement was founded around
on the shore of Taal Lake, but after it was destroyed by a major eruption of Taal Volcano in

, residents moved to the hilltop where the town now stands. Landowning families who later built wealth in the sugar, coffee, and textile trades constructed large, ornate mansions from the late Spanish era through American rule, shaping the elegant streetscape seen today.
The heart of the town is Taal Basilica (the Minor Basilica of St. Martin of Tours), rising atop the hill. Begun in
and completed in
, the church is about
long and about
wide, with a dome about

high, making it the largest church building in the Philippines, and it is often described as "the largest Catholic church in Asia." From the plaza in front of the church, you can look down on old mansions with red tile roofs and wooden balconies lining the alleys, with Balayan Bay in the distance.
Taal is home to many houses linked to figures of the Philippine independence movement. The birthplace of Marcela Agoncillo, who hand-sewed the first Philippine flag in Hong Kong in

, and the house of the Apacible brothers — Leon Apacible, a revolutionary-era lawyer and member of the Malolos Congress, and Galicano Apacible, a physician and president of the reform group La Solidaridad — are open as museums of the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP). The town center (poblacion), where the basilica and old mansions are clustered, was designated a National Historical Landmark zone in

Recommended for travelers who'd rather stroll quiet old-town alleys than a crowded tourist spot, for those who love architecture and photography, and for anyone interested in Philippine Catholic culture and independence history. It's about
1 hour
by car from Tagaytay, so pairing the two places into a
1-night, 2-day
trip is a popular plan.
The route is simple. Start at the hilltop plaza with the basilica and the municipal hall (the former Casa Real,
), follow Marcela Agoncillo Street past museums and old mansions, then take the San Lorenzo Ruiz Steps down to the Caysasay district by the Pansipit River. Seeing just the key sights on foot takes
3–4 hours
, while taking your time inside the museums fills a whole day. The National Historical Commission museums are closed on Mondays, so it's best to visit Tuesday through Sunday.

A huge church built of coral stone and brick, with an overwhelming high vaulted ceiling and long nave inside. In the past you could pay a small fee to climb the bell tower and look down on the town and Balayan Bay, but some recent visitors report that access to the tower has been closed, so check on site whether it is open.

blocks.title: Our Lady of Caysasay Church and the San Lorenzo Ruiz Steps

children.text: A small church steeped in the legend that a fisherman pulled a statue of the Virgin Mary out of the Pansipit River in
. You reach it by descending 125 stone steps (the San Lorenzo Ruiz Steps) from the basilica. It reopened in
June 2024
after four years of restoration and was declared a National Historical Landmark on the same day.
An arched stone well in the woods near Caysasay Church, said to be near where the statue of the Virgin was found. Pilgrims come to wash their eyes with its water, believed to cure illness.

The birthplace of the woman who made the Philippine flag, displaying period furniture, household items, and the story of the flag's creation. In the backyard stands a statue of mother and daughter sewing the flag.
A private museum inside a converted old mansion, holding vintage cameras and old photographs from the 19th century to the present. A great window into the everyday life of old Taal through pictures.

Known as the "Wedding Gift House," this 19th-century mansion is said to have been built by a wealthy groom as a gift for his bride. Depending on when you visit, interior tours and a traditional merienda (afternoon snack) experience are sometimes offered.

blocks.title: Taal food and traditional crafts shopping

children.text: In the town market and souvenir shops, look for garlicky Taal longganisa, sweet-and-savory Taal tapa, peanut brittle panucha, traditional embroidered (burda) handkerchiefs, and butterfly balisong knives.
The former home of the Apacible brothers on Marcela Agoncillo Street, run free of charge by the National Historical Commission. Around
it was a gathering place for reformists and revolutionaries, and it now displays exhibits on the brothers' lives and the revolutionary era. Open Tuesday to Sunday, closed on Mondays.

When it rains, the San Lorenzo Ruiz Steps and the path toward Caysasay get slippery, and the riverside can flood. Visit Caysasay Church and Santa Lucia Well by tricycle after the rain stops.

If you're heading straight from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA), take a taxi or Grab to PITX (Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange), about
20–30 minutes
, and board a bus to Lemery (about

). PITX has fewer Lemery departures than Buendia, so check the last bus time at the terminal first; if your flight lands late in the afternoon, it's easier to stay a night in Manila and set out the next morning.
About
120km
from Manila. Take the South Luzon Expressway (SLEX) and the STAR Tollway toward Batangas, exiting around Lipa or Batangas City onto the national road toward Lemery and Taal. It takes about
2 hours 30 minutes

It's about
50km
from Tagaytay to Taal, roughly
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
by car. Public transport requires transferring between jeepneys or vans toward Lemery, which is inconvenient, so Grab or a chartered vehicle is recommended.
From Lipa, take a jeepney bound for Lemery from SM Lipa Grand Terminal and get off at the Taal entrance (about
one way). From Batangas City, jeepneys to Lemery and buses to Nasugbu pass through Bauan and San Luis and along the national highway at the Taal entrance, taking about
1 hour
. From the highway to the town center, take a tricycle.
The town center has its main sights within a
radius of the basilica, so it's walkable. Still, with many hills and steps, an hourly tricycle charter (about
per hour) is sometimes used on hot days to tour the old mansions.
The
November–April
dry season is best for walking. Especially in
December–February
, low humidity and cool breezes make climbing the hills and steps comfortable.
March–May
can push midday temperatures to 34–35°C, so it's best to start early in the morning and rest in indoor museums and restaurants at midday. During the
June–October
rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent, and typhoons crossing the Batangas coast bring strong winds and heavy rain.
The most special time to see Taal is during its religious festivals. On Good Friday of Holy Week (the week before Easter, usually
late March–April

), dozens of flower-decked carrozas carrying statues of saints wind through town by candlelight in a grand procession, known as one of the most notable Holy Week processions in the Philippines. The feast of St. Martin on
November 11
is the town's biggest festival day, and on the feast of Our Lady of Caysasay in
early December
, a fluvial procession carries the statue of the Virgin by boat along the Pansipit River. Lodging and parking run short during these periods, so plan ahead. Every year around
March
April

in some years), the El Pasubat festival — named after the first letters of empanada, longganisa, panucha, suman, balisong, barong, and tapa — features a parade of floats topped with giant suman and balisong replicas and a street dance competition.

If the alert level of nearby Taal Volcano is raised, volcanic gas warnings may be issued for lakeside areas, so check announcements from the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS). In
April 2026
, a minor phreatic eruption occurred on Volcano Island, but the alert stayed at Level 1 (low-level unrest). Even at Level 1, entry to Volcano Island (the Permanent Danger Zone) is prohibited.

Taal is small and doesn't have much lodging, but a few heritage guesthouses and B&Bs in converted old mansions let you spend a night in a 19th-century atmosphere (about
a night). For more options, there are hotels in downtown Lemery (about
), about
15–20 minutes
away by car, or resorts in Tagaytay, about
1 hour
away.

Taal is the home of Batangas cuisine. Taal longganisa is a short, plump sausage that's not sweet but strongly garlicky — the classic way to eat it is "longsilog," paired with fried egg and garlic rice for breakfast. Also be sure to try the sweet-and-savory cured beef or pork "Taal tapa," the turmeric-tinted "adobong dilaw," and fried tawilis, a freshwater sardine found only in Taal Lake. For dessert, enjoy chewy suman (sticky rice cakes) and peanut brittle panucha with Batangas's specialty kapeng barako coffee. Most of this can be enjoyed affordably at the market and restaurant row near the basilica.
For lodging, the best known is Paradores del Castillo, a converted early-1900s mansion on Del Castillo Street near the San Lorenzo Ruiz Steps, at around

a night including breakfast. Among restaurants, Don Juan Boodle House next to the public market is the long-standing favorite, famous for its boodle spreads — tapa, longganisa, fried tawilis, and adobong dilaw laid out on banana leaves and shared by hand. Gifts such as longganisa, tapa, suman, and panucha are cheapest at the Taal Public Market in the town center, and you can also buy embroidered handkerchiefs and barong Tagalog in and around the market.
Taal Basilica and its plaza photograph best with the morning sun facing them directly. We recommend arriving before
Some heritage-house museums close on Mondays or during lunch hour (
), so check operating hours on the Facebook page or on-site signage before visiting.
The town's restaurants, museums, and tricycles mostly take cash only. ATMs are scarce, so bring plenty of cash from Manila.
With so many hills and stone steps, flat, comfortable sneakers are essential. The stone steps are very slippery after rain.
When visiting the church, avoid sleeveless tops and short shorts, and view quietly from the back during Mass.
Vacuum-packed longganisa and tapa travel well back to Manila. Bringing a cooler bag adds extra peace of mind.
Most old mansions are private homes. Photograph only the exterior of houses that aren't open museums, and don't go inside.
If visiting during Holy Week or a feast day, ask the parish office in advance about the procession's start time, and arrive
1 hour
early for a good spot.
Admission to the Villavicencio Mansion and Galeria Taal is about

each (guided explanation included), while the Marcela Agoncillo Historical Landmark and Leon Apacible Historical Landmark run by the National Historical Commission, the Basilica, and Caysasay Church are free. Galeria Taal is open Tuesday to Sunday from
8 AM to 5 PM
Tourist information for Taal is available on the
official Taal website
; its Heritage Village section lists the names of 24 old mansions and museums, which is handy when planning your route.

Taal's signature balisong (butterfly knife) is a bladed weapon whose public carry is restricted in the Philippines. If you buy one as a souvenir, pack it only in checked luggage, and check your home country's import rules for bladed weapons beforehand.
Tricycles and vehicles move quickly through the narrow alleys and national road, so be careful not to stand in the road while taking photos.
During the rainy season and typhoon period, the low-lying Pansipit riverside can flood, making the steps and path to Caysasay Church dangerous.
Some old wooden mansions have weak floors and stairs in places — stay only in accessible areas, and hold children's hands.
Climbing steps in the midday heat can cause dehydration easily, so drink water often.
Tricycles have no meters and sometimes quote tourists high fares, so agree on the destination and fare before getting in, and for hourly charters, confirm the stops and duration in advance.
A balisong (butterfly knife) is banned from carry-on luggage even as a souvenir, and may be classified as a bladed weapon by customs in your home country. Be sure to check import rules before buying.
